text: So what is an LLM gateway?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: An LLM gateway is an entry point or a middleware between your apps and the model providers behind them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It does a bunch of things, routing, authentication, fallback, rate limits, all kinds of governance that you can think of.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And right at the heart of the gateway is a fight between four things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's availability, latency, your guardrails, and costs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In case of a degradation, you cannot maximize all four.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You need to pick what you want.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So with this talk,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you use an LLM gateway, I want to help you to make that trade-off for your use case.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if you design a gateway, I want you to design or provide those levers to your callers and customers so that your customers are happy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Let's start with availability.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you have a single model provider, their ceiling is your ceiling.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Their outage is your outage.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So in typical software engineering, the way you tackle unreliable dependency is by retrying, retrying with exponential backups, with jitters.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And when all of that fails, you have a circuit breaker that trips after you've seen sufficient failures, and you stop calling the damn thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is not enough for LLMs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: LLMs are very different compared to your fast, cheap APIs that you retry on.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Retrying an LLM API eats into your latency budget really fast.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And also, tripping over a circuit breaker when you have another perfectly fine model provider to route to doesn't make sense.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You should use the second model provider.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And third, as I said, the calls are slow and expensive.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So blind retries just multiply your cost and your tail latencies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what is a better idea here?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It is actually a per-request fallback.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What that means is you can actually try model provider A and then in sequence try model provider B if your request model provider A fails.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Another option to consider here is you can fire requests to both the providers in parallel, but that's only if you're highly, highly obsessed with latencies, because that's just going to double your cost.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some of the similar circuit-breaking patterns apply here to LLMs as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you know that your primary has been failing for some time, it doesn't make sense to try it again.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You take it out of the load balancer or your request path and put it in a cool down, and then after a few minutes have passed, try putting that back again.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One interesting choice that you have to make here is where your failure counts live.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can decide to have the failure counts live in memory on the instances that are serving your traffic, or you can have shared infra where your
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Failure counts are shared across the fleet.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There are trade-offs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you want quick failovers, then fleet-wide helps.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And with instance, with local state counters, the issue that you run into is whenever you change your deployment size, your configuration and your expectations change.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So something to consider.

text: So with LLM gateways, you can have a normalization layer that can ensure that you can do cross-provider fallbacks as well.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I would like to call out one other thing where I've seen teams trip over and over again.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: To keep your model secure, you need to have guardrails.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And with that, guardrails are necessary for preventing your services from prompt injection attacks, keeping PII filters in place, having toxicity filters, keeping the LLMs to stop swearing at your customers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All those good things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But just like a model provider, there are trade-offs, too.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Guardrails are just like another service.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That can go down.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That can be unreliable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's where you need to choose.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Do you fail open or do you fail close?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When I say fail open, you can still serve the request even if your guardrails are down.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Fail close, you block the request and say, hey, I'm not available.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's the trade-off between availability and security to a certain extent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: While there's a no universal answer, it really depends on your use case.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can decide, like, for example, a toxicity filter, if it's not up and running, you can still serve that request.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the default choice should be the worst case that you can live with.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There are a few things that you can actually do to improve the behavior of your systems in face of guardrails being down and managing just unreliability of the guardrails themselves.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the first is time budget.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your request should never be bound by your guardrail timing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It should always be the LLM that is the rate determining step.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So make sure that you have timeouts in place, and those guardrails run with a specific time budget.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Another important thing is fallback.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You've heard, you probably know, and I've talked about it, we always discuss fallbacks with regards to model providers, but guardrails are critical services too, where you can consider fallbacks, have secondary providers, secondary checks, cash decisions to keep your service available when
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A guardrail provider is down.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Another interesting choice that pops up with regards to guardrails is the placement of the guardrails.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Typically, you can place the guardrail in three ways.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can have a prehook where the guardrail actually runs on the input, and that's probably the safest, but it does add serial latency to your requests.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Another one is in parallel.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is one of my favorites, but just to call out, streaming wouldn't work well here with parallel.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So if you're specially producing structured output, please don't stream them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Try to save your latencies and run these guardrails concurrently for your structured outputs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Another one is post hooks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These are best for output monitoring, auditing your outputs, and so forth.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, so far, I've discussed all the things that can go wrong with regards to our dependencies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We haven't discussed that we are actually adding another dependency in the request path itself, which is the central or which is the LLM gateway itself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There are a few things where we have been bitten by and we've learned some lessons that I want to share with you if you're working on an LLM gateway or using one.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One is shared limits.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Make sure that your API keys are segregated per route, per use case, to the most granular thing that you can imagine.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Having a noisy tenant can be one of the biggest problems here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Another thing is load shedding.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is a feature that you should, as part of your run books, game days, make sure that the gateway that you're using supports load shedding.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because when you have a retry storm, it becomes really hard to just scale out.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You cannot simply scale out services that is under a retry storm.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And all these web servers, they have an internal queue, and they're configurable, make sure that they're bounded, and they cannot accept requests that are unbounded.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if you want to have some custom logic, you can even have traffic prioritization here as well to make sure under load your most important use cases get served well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Last thing that I wanted to discuss is the whole idea of a central gateway itself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It is a single point of failure.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So if you're thinking of having a central gateway for your entire company for two LLMs, I would recommend re-think that and see what are the reasons that you want it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What I've noticed is that in most scenarios, it's not the central gateway that they want.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They want centralized governance.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And there is a path forward where you can actually decentralize the gateway and still centralize governance.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So do not try to centralize your traffic, but you can have plugins, you can have custom code that can centralize your governance.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Governance can be in the form of cost tracking, rate limit management, and there are other solutions possible.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So explore those before you chart on
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: having one central gateway for your entire company.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It can be managed by a single team, but I wouldn't recommend deploying it as a single deployment for the entire company, even though it's distributed.
